tagline: A freeway climbs past Fortuna through hills, rock cuts and habitat
intro: SR 52 crosses Mission Trails Regional Park as a freeway, climbing to Mission Trails Pass north of Fortuna Mountain. Caltrans designated the stretch between Santo Road and Mast Boulevard a scenic highway in 2016. The Mission Trails Regional Park Foundation describes a landscape of rugged hills, valleys and open areas. Road cuts expose Eocene rocks estimated at 50 million years old, with marine fossils; farther east, the road cuts through granite thought to be 150 million years old.

Plans for the La Jolla–Santee route date to 1959, but the freeway reached completion only in 2011. East of Santo Road, objections concerned both the endangered least Bell’s vireo’s habitat and the loss of homes and businesses. Construction toward Mission Gorge Road began in 1991 and included a new 45-acre songbird habitat as mitigation. Funding problems delayed the final extension. The crossing opened to Mission Gorge Road in 1993; the freeway reached SR 125 in 1998, with the remaining extension to SR 67 opening in 2011.

Traveling east, Santo Road marks the Tierrasanta approach to the park crossing. A separate two-way bicycle path follows the freeway’s north side to Mast Boulevard. Beyond that interchange, the freeway crosses the San Diego River and begins following it into Santee.

moments.title: Fortuna Mountain
moments.text: Fortuna rises above lower mesas, making it visible from SR 52 as the freeway crosses between San Diego and Santee. Also called North Fortuna, it is the northernmost of the five peaks dominating the park’s center. The freeway passes north of the mountain. Hiking routes from the Old Mission Dam area climb the saddle between North and South Fortuna, then turn north along the summit ridge. From the summit, the view includes San Diego and Santee, with Cowles Mountain to the south and the Cuyamaca Mountains to the east.
moments.notice: Fortuna stands above the surrounding lower mesas.

moments.title: Old Mission Dam
moments.text: The surviving stone-and-cement dam belongs to an irrigation system built to carry San Diego River water to the fields of Mission San Diego de Alcalá. Built in 1803, it stored water for controlled releases when the seasonal river ran dry. A tiled channel reduced water loss through sandy soil on the way to the fields. The dam and aqueduct were reported in ruins in 1867; repairs put the dam back to use in 1874. Only fragments of the channel survive, alongside the dam remnant designated a National Historic Landmark in 1963.
moments.notice: The surviving dam is built of stone and cement.

moments.title: Kumeyaay Lake
moments.text: Kumeyaay Lake occupies a former gravel pit within Mission Trails Regional Park. Its habitat includes riparian and chaparral plants. The small lake has a campground beside it, part of a park that also contains the San Diego River.
